# Computational Evidence — Co-Wellfounded Chains and Direct Sums

Focused evidence for the three formalized results, obtained by evaluating small
order models.

## 1. Small-case models for Theorem 1 (`chain_finite_of_wf_cowf`)

A chain is classified by whether it admits an infinite ascending / descending
sequence. "coWF" = co-wellfounded = no infinite ascending sequence; "WF" = well
founded = no infinite descending sequence.

| chain        | WF? | coWF? | finite? | consistent with T1 |
|--------------|-----|-------|---------|--------------------|
| `Fin 0..n`   | yes | yes   | yes     | ✅ (WF∧coWF ⇒ finite) |
| `ℕ`          | yes | no    | no      | ✅ (coWF fails)      |
| `ℕᵒᵈ` (`ω*`) | no  | yes   | no      | ✅ (WF fails)        |
| `ℤ`          | no  | no    | no      | ✅                   |
| `ω + ω*`     | no  | no    | no      | ✅                   |

No infinite chain in the sample is simultaneously WF and coWF: every infinite
linear order exhibits an infinite monotone sequence in at least one direction,
exactly as the Erdős–Szekeres dichotomy predicts.

## 2. Witness for Theorem 2 (`infinite_cowf_chain_has_descending`)

Take `α = ℕᵒᵈ` (`ω*`). It is infinite and co-wellfounded (ascending chains in
`ℕᵒᵈ` correspond to descending chains in `ℕ`, which terminate). The explicit
descending sequence is `f n = (n : ℕ)` viewed in `ℕᵒᵈ`:
`f 0 > f 1 > f 2 > …`, i.e. a copy of `ω*`. This confirms an infinite
co-wellfounded chain always carries an infinite strictly descending sequence.

## 3. Direct sums for Theorem 3 (`directSum_not_isFAC`)

For `β : ι → Poset`, the direct sum `Σ i, β i` compares two points only inside a
common summand.

| index `ι` | summands            | largest antichain | FAC? |
|-----------|---------------------|-------------------|------|
| `Fin 1`   | `ℕ`                 | 1                 | yes  |
| `Fin 2`   | `ℕ, ℕ`              | 2                 | yes  |
| `Fin k`   | any nonempty        | k                 | yes  |
| `ℕ`       | `Unit` each         | ∞ (whole space)   | **no** |
| `ℕ`       | `ℕ` each            | ∞ (`{⟨n,0⟩}`)      | **no** |

The transition to an infinite index destroys FAC: one point per summand is an
infinite antichain. Finite direct sums stay FAC, so the break is precisely at
`|ι| ≥ ω`.

## 4. Counterexample hunt

* "coWF ⇒ WF for chains": refuted by `ω*` (coWF, not WF).
* "every FAC chain is finite": refuted by `ℕ` (a chain has no 2-element
  antichain, so it is FAC, yet infinite).
* "direct sum of FAC posets is FAC": refuted by countably many copies of `Unit`.

No counterexample was found to any of the three formalized theorems.

## 5. Relation to sequences / OEIS

The only counting quantity appearing is the maximal antichain size of a finite
direct sum of `k` nonempty posets, which is simply `k` (OEIS A000027, the natural
numbers) — a sanity check rather than a discovery.

# Future Directions

Bold, falsifiable conjectures growing out of this cycle's study of chains,
antichains, co-wellfoundedness, and direct sums.

## 1. The two-sided failure of welded co-wellfounded chains

Weld countably many infinite reverse-well-ordered chains end to end, in order
type indexed by the natural numbers, to obtain a single saturated chain. Then
neither this chain nor its reverse is well founded, and the ascending sequences
responsible for the failure live entirely across the welding seams rather than
inside any block.

**The key insight is** that co-wellfoundedness is a strictly one-directional
property, so gluing one-directional pieces along a second direction inevitably
manufactures the missing infinite ascending sequence at the block boundaries.

**Why now?** We have just isolated, in complete rigor, the atomic fact that every
infinite co-wellfounded chain carries a copy of the reverse of the natural
numbers. That atom is exactly what a block-wise gluing argument needs, so the
step from single chains to welded chains is finally within reach.

## 2. Additivity of the finite antichain condition under finite direct sums

Combining finitely many posets that each forbid infinite antichains again forbids
infinite antichains, and the largest antichain of the combination is exactly the
sum of the largest antichains of the parts.

**The key insight is** that any antichain of a disjoint combination splits as the
union of its restrictions to the individual parts, so finiteness and size add
across finitely many parts and only diverge once infinitely many parts appear.

**Why now?** We have proved the negative threshold — infinitely many nonempty
parts always create an infinite antichain — so pinning down the exact positive
regime just below that threshold is the natural and immediately actionable
counterpart.

## 3. A chain-or-antichain dichotomy sharpening the monotone-sequence theorem

Every infinite partial order contains either an infinite chain or an infinite
antichain, and a partial order is finite if and only if it simultaneously
forbids infinite ascending sequences, infinite descending sequences, and
infinite antichains.

**The key insight is** that the two-colouring of pairs by "comparable versus
incomparable" turns the classical monotone-subsequence argument into a Ramsey
statement whose monochromatic sets are precisely chains and antichains.

**Why now?** Our finiteness theorem already covers the linear case using a
two-way monotone dichotomy; adding the incomparable colour is the one extra
ingredient needed to lift it to all posets, and the infinite Ramsey machinery to
do so is standard.

## 4. Unique co-wellfounded segmentation of saturated chains

Inside any countable order with no infinite antichain, every saturated chain
breaks canonically into consecutive segments, each of which is well founded or
co-wellfounded, and the obstruction to the fibre-partition property is the
presence of infinitely many infinite co-wellfounded segments.

**The key insight is** that saturation makes segment boundaries respect the
covering relation, so the segment types become genuine order invariants rather
than artefacts of a chosen presentation.

**Why now?** With co-wellfounded segments now understood in isolation, defining
and proving invariance of the segmentation is the concrete next milestone toward
a structural characterization of which chains obstruct the fibre-partition
property.

## 5. Antichain width as a numeric separator between direct and linear sums

Assign to each order the growth rate of the largest antichain among its finite
sub-configurations. Direct sums make this rate grow, linear sums leave it fixed,
and boundedness of the rate is equivalent to forbidding infinite antichains.

**The key insight is** that the two ways of combining posets used throughout this
subject — disjoint (direct) and consecutive (linear) — are told apart by a single
monotone numerical invariant, turning a structural distinction into a
quantitative one.

**Why now?** We now have both endpoints in hand: infinite direct sums force
unbounded width while chains keep width one, so the intermediate calibration is a
well-posed and timely quantitative program.

-- NEW_FILE: a793b4d3_retry1_aristotle/Combinatorics/BooleanChainCover.lean
import Mathlib

/-!
# Chain cover lower bound for the Boolean lattice `B_n = Finset (Fin n)`

This file proves, from first principles (Finset API, basic set theory, pigeonhole),
that any family of chains whose union covers the Boolean lattice `Finset (Fin n)`
must contain at least `n.choose (n / 2)` chains.

The argument deliberately avoids Dilworth's theorem and any theorem about *minimum*
chain covers: the chain-cover bound is derived FROM the antichain intersection lemma
(`inter_subsingleton_of_isChain_of_isAntichain`), not the other way around.

## Main statements

* `inter_subsingleton_of_isChain_of_isAntichain` : a chain meets an antichain in at
  most one point.
* `middleLayer_isAntichain` : the middle layer `{s | s.card = n / 2}` is an antichain.
* `middleLayer_card` : the middle layer has `n.choose (n / 2)` elements.
* `chain_cover_card_ge_middle` : any chain cover has at least `n.choose (n / 2)` chains.
-/

open Finset

namespace BooleanChainCover

variable {n : ℕ}

/-- The middle layer of the Boolean lattice `Finset (Fin n)`: all subsets of
cardinality `n / 2`. -/
def middleLayer (n : ℕ) : Finset (Finset (Fin n)) :=
  Finset.univ.filter (fun s => s.card = n / 2)

/-
**Lemma 1 (antichain intersection).**
A chain `C` and an antichain `A` (both ordered by `⊆`) intersect in at most one
element.  If `x, y ∈ C ∩ A` were distinct, the chain property would force
`x ⊆ y` or `y ⊆ x`, contradicting `A` being an antichain.
-/
lemma inter_subsingleton_of_isChain_of_isAntichain
    {C A : Finset (Finset (Fin n))}
    (hC : IsChain (· ⊆ ·) (C : Set (Finset (Fin n))))
    (hA : IsAntichain (· ⊆ ·) (A : Set (Finset (Fin n)))) :
    (C ∩ A).card ≤ 1 := by
  by_contra h_contra; push_neg at h_contra; (
  obtain ⟨ x, hx, y, hy, hxy ⟩ := Finset.one_lt_card.mp h_contra; have := hC.total ( Finset.mem_of_mem_inter_left hx ) ( Finset.mem_of_mem_inter_left hy ) ; simp_all +decide [ IsAntichain ] ;
  cases this <;> have := hA hx.2 hy.2 <;> aesop);

/-
**Lemma 2 (the middle layer is an antichain).**
If `s, t` both have cardinality `n / 2` and `s ⊆ t`, then `s = t` by cardinality,
so distinct middle-layer sets are incomparable.
-/
theorem middleLayer_isAntichain (n : ℕ) :
    IsAntichain (· ⊆ ·) (middleLayer n : Set (Finset (Fin n))) := by
  intro s hs t ht hst;
  simp_all +decide [ middleLayer ];
  exact fun h => hst <| Finset.eq_of_subset_of_card_le h <| by linarith;

/-
**Lemma 3 (size of the middle layer).**
The middle layer has exactly `n.choose (n / 2)` elements.
-/
theorem middleLayer_card (n : ℕ) : (middleLayer n).card = n.choose (n / 2) := by
  unfold middleLayer; aesop;

/-
**Theorem 4 (chain cover lower bound).**
If `F` is a family of chains (each `C ∈ F` is a chain under `⊆`) whose union
covers every subset of `Fin n`, then `F` contains at least `n.choose (n / 2)`
chains.

The proof is a pigeonhole argument: the middle layer `A` is an antichain with
`|A| = n.choose (n / 2)`; each chain meets `A` in at most one element
(Lemma 1); since the chains cover `A`, we get `|A| ≤ ∑_{C ∈ F} |C ∩ A| ≤ |F|`.
-/
theorem chain_cover_card_ge_middle
    {F : Finset (Finset (Finset (Fin n)))}
    (hchains : ∀ C ∈ F, IsChain (· ⊆ ·) (C : Set (Finset (Fin n))))
    (hcover : ∀ s : Finset (Fin n), s ∈ F.biUnion id) :
    n.choose (n / 2) ≤ F.card := by
  -- By Lemma 1, each chain in F intersects the middle layer in at most one element.
  have h_inter : ∀ C ∈ F, (C ∩ middleLayer n).card ≤ 1 := by
    exact fun C hC => inter_subsingleton_of_isChain_of_isAntichain ( hchains C hC ) ( middleLayer_isAntichain n );
  -- By Lemma 2, the union of all chains in F covers the middle layer.
  have h_union : middleLayer n ⊆ F.biUnion (fun C => C ∩ middleLayer n) := by
    intro s hs; specialize hcover s; aesop;
  exact le_trans ( middleLayer_card n ▸ Finset.card_le_card h_union ) ( Finset.card_biUnion_le.trans ( Finset.sum_le_card_nsmul _ _ _ fun x hx => h_inter x hx ) ) |> le_trans <| by norm_num;

end BooleanChainCover

# Computational Evidence — Chain Covers in the Boolean Lattice

We study the minimum number of chains needed to cover the Boolean lattice
`B_n = (2^{[n]}, ⊆)`, and two lower bounds for it:

- **Sperner/Dilworth bound:** `#chains ≥ C(n, ⌊n/2⌋)` (width = size of the middle layer).
- **Length/counting bound:** `2^n ≤ (n+1)·#chains`, i.e. `#chains ≥ ⌈2^n/(n+1)⌉`,
  because every chain in `B_n` has at most `n+1` elements.

## 1. Small-case table

Columns: `n`, middle binomial `C(n,⌊n/2⌋)`, total subsets `2^n`, and the counting
lower bound `⌈2^n/(n+1)⌉`.

| n | C(n,⌊n/2⌋) | 2^n | ⌈2^n/(n+1)⌉ |
|---|-----------|-----|-------------|
| 0 | 1  | 1   | 1  |
| 1 | 1  | 2   | 1  |
| 2 | 2  | 4   | 2  |
| 3 | 3  | 8   | 2  |
| 4 | 6  | 16  | 4  |
| 5 | 10 | 32  | 6  |
| 6 | 20 | 64  | 10 |
| 7 | 35 | 128 | 16 |
| 8 | 70 | 256 | 29 |

(Computed with `#eval (List.range 9).map (fun n => (n, Nat.choose n (n/2), 2^n, (2^n+n)/(n+1)))`.)

Observations:
- The middle binomial `C(n,⌊n/2⌋)` is always `≥` the counting bound `⌈2^n/(n+1)⌉`
  — consistent with the fact that the Sperner width is the *exact* minimum chain
  cover (Dilworth + symmetric chain decomposition), which must dominate any other
  lower bound. This is the empirical shadow of `middle_choose_mul_ge`
  (`2^n ≤ (n+1)·C(n,⌊n/2⌋)`).
- Both quantities grow like `2^n` up to a polynomial `n` factor:
  `C(n,⌊n/2⌋) = Θ(2^n / √n)` (central binomial), while the crude counting bound
  is `Θ(2^n / n)`. So the log-scale gap between the two lower bounds is
  `½ log₂ n + O(1)` — a genuinely *logarithmic* deficit, matching the "logarithmic
  approximation" theme.

## 2. Sanity checks of the extremal antichain (middle layer)

- n=2: middle layer = `{ {0}, {1} }`, size `2 = C(2,1)`; it is an antichain, and
  `B_2` is covered by the two chains `∅ ⊂ {0} ⊂ {0,1}` and `{1}` — so 2 chains
  are necessary (this antichain) and sufficient. Minimum = 2 = C(2,1). ✓
- n=3: middle layer = all 3 singletons and (for `⌊3/2⌋=1`) the size-1 sets;
  `C(3,1)=3`. A symmetric chain decomposition of `B_3` uses exactly 3 chains. ✓
- n=4: `C(4,2)=6`; symmetric chain decomposition uses exactly 6 chains. ✓

## 3. Counterexample hunt

- Claim "`2^n ≤ (n+1)·C(n,⌊n/2⌋)`" tested for `n ≤ 8`: holds in every row
  (`1≤1, 2≤2, 4≤6, 8≤12, 16≤30, 32≤60, 64≤140, 128≤280, 256≤630`). No
  counterexample. This is the finite reflection of the proved theorem
  `middle_choose_mul_ge`.
- Claim "every chain in `B_n` has `≤ n+1` elements" — a chain is strictly
  monotone in cardinality, and cardinalities lie in `{0,…,n}`, so at most `n+1`
  values; no counterexample possible (proved as `chain_card_le`).

## 4. OEIS

The middle-binomial sequence `1, 1, 2, 3, 6, 10, 20, 35, 70, …` is
**OEIS A001405** (central binomial coefficients `C(n, ⌊n/2⌋)`), which is exactly
the minimum number of chains in a chain cover / the maximum antichain size of the
Boolean lattice `B_n`.

## Conclusion

The computations corroborate all four formalized results and, in particular, the
ordering `⌈2^n/(n+1)⌉ ≤ C(n,⌊n/2⌋) ≤ minimum chain cover`, with a logarithmic
`Θ(√n)` multiplicative gap between the two lower bounds.

# Future Directions — Chain Covers in the Boolean Lattice

Five bold, falsifiable conjectures growing out of this cycle's findings on the
minimum number of chains needed to cover the lattice of subsets of an
`n`-element set ordered by inclusion.

## 1. The optimum is exactly the middle layer, achieved by a canonical bracketing

**Conjecture.** The minimum number of chains required to cover the subset lattice
of an `n`-element set is exactly the central binomial coefficient
`C(n, ⌊n/2⌋)`, and it is attained by the symmetric chain decomposition obtained
from the classical parenthesis-matching rule on characteristic strings.

The key insight is that the pigeonhole bound against the middle antichain and the
explicit bracketing construction meet at the same number, so no covering can beat
the widest antichain and none needs to exceed it. **Why now?** We have already
pinned the lower bound to `C(n, ⌊n/2⌋)`; the missing half is a single explicit
construction whose correctness is a finite, checkable combinatorial invariant,
making this the natural next milestone.

## 2. A logarithmic deficit separates the two natural lower bounds

**Conjecture.** The ratio between the sharp width `C(n, ⌊n/2⌋)` and the crude
counting estimate `2^n/(n+1)` grows exactly like `c·√n` with
`c = √(π/2) + o(1)`, so on a logarithmic scale the two lower bounds differ by
`½·log₂ n + O(1)`.

The key insight is that the length bound "every chain has at most `n+1` links"
loses a full `√n` factor compared with the antichain bound, and this loss is
governed precisely by the central-limit spreading of the binomial coefficients.
**Why now?** Both bounds are already in hand and agree up to a polynomial factor;
isolating the exact constant turns a qualitative gap into a sharp quantitative
law and clarifies when cheap length arguments suffice.

## 3. Divisor lattices inherit a multiplicative chain-cover law

**Conjecture.** For an integer with prime factorization exponents
`e_1, …, e_k`, the minimum number of chains covering its divisor lattice equals
the largest coefficient of the polynomial
`(1 + x + … + x^{e_1})···(1 + x + … + x^{e_k})`; for squarefree integers this
specializes to `C(k, ⌊k/2⌋)`.

The key insight is that a divisor lattice is a product of chains, so its widest
antichain is the middle-weight layer, whose size is exactly the peak coefficient
of the associated Gaussian product polynomial. **Why now?** The squarefree case
is already understood as the Boolean lattice, and the product structure gives an
immediate, testable generalization that ties multiplicative number theory to
extremal order theory.

## 4. Random sublattices concentrate their chain-cover number

**Conjecture.** If each subset of an `n`-element set is kept independently with
probability `p`, then the minimum number of chains covering the kept subsets is,
with high probability, `(1 + o(1))·p·C(n, ⌊n/2⌋)`, and there is a sharp threshold
in `p` above which the retained middle layer alone forces a cover of order
`2^n/√n`.

The key insight is that the middle layer is so much larger than every other rank
that even after random thinning it still dominates the width, so the cover number
tracks the surviving fraction of that single layer. **Why now?** Average-case and
noisy versions of extremal set problems are increasingly central to
sampling-based data structures, and the extreme concentration of mass on the
middle rank makes a clean concentration statement plausible and checkable.

## 5. Inclusion-exclusion certificates for width lower bounds

**Conjecture.** For any graded poset with rank sizes `r_0, …, r_N` summing to
`T`, every partial alternating sum of the `r_i` yields a valid lower bound on the
maximum rank size (and hence on the chain-cover number), and for the subset
lattice the two-term certificate `T ≤ (N+1)·max_i r_i` is already tight up to the
`√n` factor of Direction 2.

The key insight is that the identity `2^n = Σ C(n,i)` bounding each term by the
maximum is a one-line inclusion-exclusion certificate, and the same alternating
bookkeeping should extend to subspace lattices, partition lattices, and truncated
Young's lattices where the peak count is a `q`-binomial or hook-length quantity.
**Why now?** We have a working two-term certificate in the Boolean case; framing
it as a general principle promises uniform, verifiable width bounds across a whole
family of lattices arising in coding theory and enumerative combinatorics.
